planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Chimacum Katie is a formal decorative dahlia from the Dan's Dahlias breeding program in Chimacum, Washington, producing large blooms blending peach, salmon, and cream tones with neatly arranged, symmetrical petals. Disbud side buds to a single terminal bud for the largest show-quality flowers and stake stems early since the heavy blooms can bend in wind and rain. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in regions colder than zone 8.

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Chimacum Patches is a novelty decorative dahlia, also from the Dan's Dahlias breeding line, prized for white petals irregularly splashed and streaked with purple-pink patches so that no two blooms look quite alike. Grow it like other large decorative dahlias, disbudding side shoots to concentrate energy into fewer, larger flowers and staking early. Deadhead regularly to keep the plant producing fresh flushes of its distinctive patterned blooms through late summer.

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Bryn Terfel is a UK-raised decorative dahlia named for the Welsh bass-baritone opera singer, bearing velvety, deep crimson-red blooms with a slight darkening toward the center. It performs well both as a garden border plant and a cut flower, holding its color without excessive fading in cool maritime climates. Stake stems as they grow, deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, and lift tubers before hard frost outside zone 8 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Impression Fabulous is a collarette dahlia from the Dutch-bred Impression series, with a single outer ring of rich purple-pink petals surrounding a contrasting creamy-white collar of smaller petaloids around the open central disc. The open flower form makes it especially attractive to pollinators compared with fully double dahlia types. Grow it in full sun with support for the bushy, free-flowering habit, and deadhead regularly to keep up a steady succession of blooms.

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Fidalgo Blacky is a decorative dahlia from the Fidalgo breeding line, named for Fidalgo Island in Washington state, with deep maroon-red petals so dark they read almost black in low light. The intense color deepens further in cool autumn weather, making it a dramatic addition to late-season borders and cut-flower arrangements. Disbud for larger blooms, stake the sturdy stems, and lift tubers for storage where winters bring hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, eyes facing up, about 4-6 inches deep.

directions: Fidalgo Supreme is a large decorative dahlia from the same Fidalgo Island, Washington breeding line as Fidalgo Blacky, producing full, high-centered blooms on strong, upright stems. It is grown both for garden display and as a show and cut flower, holding its form well once cut. Provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through summer, staking plants as they reach full height to support the heavy flower heads.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Yvonne Arnaud is a reflexed exhibition chrysanthemum, named for the French-British stage actress, with rose-pink ray florets that curve neatly downward and overlap in tidy rows from a high center to the base of the bloom. Pinch once in late spring to establish a single terminal bud, remove competing side buds, and stake early to support the finished flower head. Grown mainly by National Chrysanthemum Society exhibitors, it benefits from protection from heavy rain as the bloom develops.

common_name: Mayford Perfection Chrysanthemum (Large Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Mayford Perfection is a classic large incurve exhibition chrysanthemum, bred in England in the early twentieth century, with bronze-orange florets that curl tightly inward to build a dense, globe-shaped bloom. It remains grown today by heritage-minded exhibitors for its reliable, perfectly symmetrical form when disbudded to a single terminal flower. Stake the tall stems early, feed regularly through summer, and protect the finished bloom from rain and direct sun to preserve its even color.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring so the mounding habit has a full season to fill out before fall bloom.

directions: White Igloo is a cold-hardy cushion-mound garden mum from the Igloo series, self-branching into a tidy dome of foliage that becomes smothered in small double white daisy flowers in autumn. Unlike exhibition types, it needs no pinching or disbudding to form its naturally rounded shape, making it a low-maintenance choice for borders and containers. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, dense growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring so the mounding habit has a full season to fill out before fall bloom.

directions: Yellow Igloo is a bright golden-yellow sibling in the cold-hardy Igloo series of cushion garden mums, forming the same tidy, self-branching dome of foliage covered in small double flowers each fall. Its compact habit holds up well under wind and rain without staking, and it tolerates colder winters than many exhibition-type mums. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring and cut plants back after a hard freeze blackens the foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring so the mounding habit has a full season to fill out before fall bloom.

directions: Coral Igloo is a soft salmon-coral flowered member of the cold-hardy Igloo cushion mum series, mounding into the same dense, self-shaping dome of foliage topped with small double flowers in autumn. Its warm coral tone pairs well with bronze and purple fall-blooming perennials in mixed borders. As with its Igloo series siblings, it needs no pinching to form its rounded habit and divides easily every two to three years in spring.
